Text.name: humor_step1_header
Text.value: 🎯 STEP 1: Look for INTENTIONAL JOKES.

Text.name: humor_step1_q
Text.value: Does the text contain any of these INTENTIONAL comedic elements?

Text.name: humor_step1_item1
Text.value: - A joke with a clear punchline or comedic setup

Text.name: humor_step1_item2
Text.value: - A pun or deliberate wordplay

Text.name: humor_step1_item3
Text.value: - A pop culture reference used for comedic effect (not just as an example)

Text.name: humor_step1_item4
Text.value: - A clearly sarcastic or mocking statement that subverts expectations

Text.name: humor_step1_ex_header
Text.value: ✓ EXAMPLES of intentional jokes (Mark Yes):

Text.name: humor_step1_ex1
Text.value: - 'Schrodinger's cat walks into a bar... and doesn't' (punchline joke)

Text.name: humor_step1_ex2
Text.value: - 'holy proofreading batman' (pop culture catchphrase used for comedic effect)

Text.name: humor_step1_ex3
Text.value: - 'you would not pass go, nor would you collect 200 dollars, you would go directly to nobel prize' (Monopoly reference twisted for humor)

Text.name: humor_step1_result
Text.value: If you found an intentional joke → Mark Yes. Otherwise continue to Step 2.

Text.name: humor_step2_header
Text.value: 🤪 STEP 2: Look for ABSURDIST or DEADPAN humor.

Text.name: humor_step2_q
Text.value: Does the text contain any of these?

Text.name: humor_step2_item1
Text.value: - An unexpected non-sequitur at the end that breaks the serious tone

Text.name: humor_step2_item2
Text.value: - A brand name, product, or random word dropped without explanation for comedic effect

Text.name: humor_step2_item3
Text.value: - A jarring tonal shift that seems intentionally funny

Text.name: humor_step2_item4
Text.value: - Self-deprecating or self-aware comments that acknowledge absurdity

Text.name: humor_step2_ex_header
Text.value: ✓ EXAMPLES of absurdist/deadpan humor (Mark Yes):

Text.name: humor_step2_ex1
Text.value: - A serious scientific answer that ends with '...and partially because **american apparel**' (non-sequitur brand drop)

Text.name: humor_step2_ex2
Text.value: - 'I'd be lying if I said I've seen it' in a technical explanation (self-aware honesty)

Text.name: humor_step2_ex3
Text.value: - 'at which point you have big problems^(tm)' (fake trademark = comedic aside)

Text.name: humor_step2_ex4
Text.value: - 'now, i must go masturbate before the shakes set in' (absurd self-deprecating callback)

Text.name: humor_step2_result
Text.value: If you found absurdist or deadpan humor → Mark Yes. Otherwise continue to Step 3.

Text.name: humor_step3_header
Text.value: 😏 STEP 3: Look for IRONY, SARCASM, or DARK HUMOR.

Text.name: humor_step3_q
Text.value: Does the text contain any of these?

Text.name: humor_step3_item1
Text.value: - Saying the opposite of what you mean with clear comedic intent

Text.name: humor_step3_item2
Text.value: - Dark understatement: making something serious sound trivially unimportant

Text.name: humor_step3_item3
Text.value: - Violent, morbid, or extreme language used casually for shock-comedy value

Text.name: humor_step3_ex_header
Text.value: ✓ EXAMPLES of irony/dark humor (Mark Yes):

Text.name: humor_step3_ex1
Text.value: - 'The surgery went well, apart from the patient dying' (dark understatement)

Text.name: humor_step3_ex2
Text.value: - 'It's perfectly safe, unless you count the possibility of horrible death' (dark humor)

Text.name: humor_step3_ex3
Text.value: - 'telescopes were played out' (ironic dismissal of something obviously important)

Text.name: humor_step3_result
Text.value: If you found clear irony or dark humor → Mark Yes. Otherwise continue to Step 4.

Text.name: humor_step4_header
Text.value: ✗ STEP 4: CRITICAL - Distinguish HUMOR from CASUAL TONE.

Text.name: humor_step4_desc
Text.value: The following are NOT humor - they are just informal/casual writing:

Text.name: humor_step4_not1
Text.value: - Candid admissions: 'I would recommend staying away from Yahoo Answers' (just honest advice)

Text.name: humor_step4_not2
Text.value: - Casual language: '[pretty good summary here]' (informal tone, not sarcasm)

Text.name: humor_step4_not3
Text.value: - Enthusiastic phrases: 'great question!' (friendly, not funny)

Text.name: humor_step4_not4
Text.value: - Mild exaggeration without comedic intent: 'scrounge up enough firepower' (vivid language)

Text.name: humor_step4_not5
Text.value: - Informal asides that don't subvert expectations: 'which is why it's not used much on earth'

Text.name: humor_step4_not6
Text.value: - Rhetorical questions: 'good question' (engaging, not joking)

Text.name: humor_key_test
Text.value: KEY TEST: Would a reader actually laugh or smile?

Text.name: humor_casual
Text.value: - Casual/informal tone = reader thinks 'that's friendly' → Mark No

Text.name: humor_intentional
Text.value: - Intentional humor = reader thinks 'that's funny' → Mark Yes

Text.name: humor_final_header
Text.value: ⚖️ FINAL DECISION:

Text.name: humor_final1
Text.value: - If you found intentional humor in Steps 1-3 that passes the laugh test → Mark Yes

Text.name: humor_final2
Text.value: - If you only found casual tone, informal language, or vivid explanations → Mark No

Text.name: conn_step1_header
Text.value: 🎨 STEP 1: Check for ANY named reference from these categories.

Text.name: conn_step1_cat_a
Text.value: A) POPULAR CULTURE:

Text.name: conn_step1_a1
Text.value: - Movies, TV shows, books, documentaries (e.g., 'Jurassic Park', 'Game of Thrones', 'The Matrix')

Text.name: conn_step1_a2
Text.value: - Music, bands, songs (e.g., 'like a Beatles song', 'Beethoven's 5th')

Text.name: conn_step1_a3
Text.value: - Video games, board games (e.g., 'Monopoly', 'Minecraft', 'chess')

Text.name: conn_step1_a4
Text.value: - Internet culture, memes, viral moments

Text.name: conn_step1_a5
Text.value: - Fictional characters (e.g., 'Batman', 'Sherlock Holmes')

Text.name: conn_step1_cat_b
Text.value: B) HISTORICAL FIGURES AND EVENTS:

Text.name: conn_step1_b1
Text.value: - Famous scientists, leaders, artists (e.g., 'Galileo', 'Einstein', 'Napoleon', 'Carl Sagan')

Text.name: conn_step1_b2
Text.value: - Historical events (e.g., 'the French Revolution', 'World War II', 'the Cold War')

Text.name: conn_step1_b3
Text.value: - Famous inventions or discoveries (e.g., 'the Tsar Bomba', 'the Manhattan Project')

Text.name: conn_step1_cat_c
Text.value: C) ORGANIZATIONS AND BRANDS:

Text.name: conn_step1_c1
Text.value: - Companies, brands, products (e.g., 'Google', 'Netflix', 'American Apparel', 'Teflon')

Text.name: conn_step1_c2
Text.value: - Government agencies (e.g., 'NASA', 'FBI', 'FCC')

Text.name: conn_step1_c3
Text.value: - Well-known institutions (e.g., 'Harvard', 'the Smithsonian')

Text.name: conn_step1_cat_d
Text.value: D) PUBLICATIONS AND MEDIA:

Text.name: conn_step1_d1
Text.value: - Magazines, newspapers (e.g., 'The Economist', 'Psychology Today', 'Time Magazine')

Text.name: conn_step1_d2
Text.value: - Websites, platforms (e.g., 'Yahoo Answers', 'Wikipedia', 'Reddit')

Text.name: conn_step1_cat_e
Text.value: E) FAMOUS PLACES:

Text.name: conn_step1_e1
Text.value: - Landmarks (e.g., 'Times Square', 'the Eiffel Tower', 'Chernobyl')

Text.name: conn_step1_e2
Text.value: - Well-known locations used as reference points

Text.name: conn_step2_header
Text.value: 🍳 STEP 2: ALSO check for concrete everyday activities.

Text.name: conn_step2_desc
Text.value: Mark Yes for relatable human experiences that ground abstract concepts:

Text.name: conn_step2_item1
Text.value: - Household tasks: 'like doing laundry', 'like vacuuming'

Text.name: conn_step2_item2
Text.value: - Food & cooking: 'like mixing cake batter', 'like grocery shopping'

Text.name: conn_step2_item3
Text.value: - Common experiences: 'like getting stuck in traffic', 'like waiting for coffee'

Text.name: conn_step2_item4
Text.value: - Childhood activities: 'like a child spinning in a circle with arms outstretched'

Text.name: conn_step2_item5
Text.value: - Social activities: 'like hosting a dinner party'

Text.name: conn_step2_key
Text.value: KEY: The activity must be something a general audience experiences personally.

Text.name: conn_step3_header
Text.value: ⚠️ STEP 3: CHECK THE 'EXTERNAL TO TOPIC' RULE.

Text.name: conn_step3_important
Text.value: IMPORTANT: The reference must be EXTERNAL to the question topic.

Text.name: conn_step3_score0_header
Text.value: ✗ Mark No if the reference is ALREADY PART of the question:

Text.name: conn_step3_score0_ex1
Text.value: - Question asks 'how has our knowledge of dinosaurs changed since Jurassic Park' → Mentioning 'Jurassic Park' does NOT count

Text.name: conn_step3_score0_ex2
Text.value: - Question asks about NASA missions → Mentioning 'NASA' does NOT count

Text.name: conn_step3_score0_ex3
Text.value: - Question asks about Einstein's theories → Mentioning 'Einstein' does NOT count

Text.name: conn_step3_score10_header
Text.value: ✓ Mark Yes if the reference is EXTERNAL:

Text.name: conn_step3_score10_ex1
Text.value: - Question about physics → Mentioning 'Galileo' DOES count (external historical figure)

Text.name: conn_step3_score10_ex2
Text.value: - Question about nuclear reactors → Mentioning 'the Cold War' or 'Tsar Bomba' DOES count

Text.name: conn_step3_score10_ex3
Text.value: - Question about space → Mentioning 'NASA' DOES count (if NASA wasn't in the question)

Text.name: conn_step4_header
Text.value: ✗ STEP 4: What does NOT count (Mark No).

Text.name: conn_step4_not1
Text.value: - Generic physics analogies: 'like a ball rolling downhill', 'like waves in water'

Text.name: conn_step4_not2
Text.value: - Nature analogies: 'like a river flowing', 'like clouds forming'

Text.name: conn_step4_not3
Text.value: - Abstract comparisons: 'like a sponge absorbing', 'like a balloon'

Text.name: conn_step4_not4
Text.value: - Vague references: 'as we all know', 'in everyday life'

Text.name: conn_step4_not5
Text.value: - Technical jargon without cultural grounding

Text.name: conn_step4_not6
Text.value: - References already embedded in the original question (see Step 3)

Text.name: conn_step5_header
Text.value: ⚖️ STEP 5: FINAL DECISION.

Text.name: conn_step5_yes_header
Text.value: Mark Yes if:

Text.name: conn_step5_yes1
Text.value: - You found ANY named reference from Step 1 categories, AND it is EXTERNAL to the question topic

Text.name: conn_step5_yes2
Text.value: - OR: You found a concrete everyday activity from Step 2 that is EXTERNAL to the question topic

Text.name: conn_step5_final_header
Text.value: FINAL EXAMPLES:

Text.name: conn_step5_final1
Text.value: - 'Galileo discovered the moons of Jupiter' in a question about CERN → Mark Yes (Galileo is external)

Text.name: conn_step5_final2
Text.value: - 'the Tsar Bomba' in a question about killing stars → Mark Yes (famous Cold War bomb, external)

Text.name: conn_step5_final3
Text.value: - 'Psychology Today' in any answer → Mark Yes (named publication)

Text.name: conn_step5_final4
Text.value: - 'like a child spinning' in a physics question → Mark Yes (relatable everyday activity)

Text.name: conn_step5_final5
Text.value: - 'Jurassic Park' in a question asking about Jurassic Park → Mark No (NOT external)

Text.name: conn_step5_no
Text.value: Mark No otherwise.

Text.name: metaphor_step1_header
Text.value: 1. DEFINITION

Text.name: metaphor_step1_item1
Text.value: A METAPHOR is ACTIVE / LIVE figurative language in which a concept is framed, evaluated, or described using another domain in a NON-LITERAL way.

Text.name: metaphor_step1_item2
Text.value: For this task, ONLY score ACTIVE metaphors.

Text.name: metaphor_step1_item3
Text.value: Conventional, idiomatic, or dead metaphors must be marked No, UNLESS they are reactivated via a clear domain shift.

Text.name: metaphor_step1_item4
Text.value: Metaphors may be imagistic OR abstract.

Text.name: metaphor_step1_item5
Text.value: Metaphors may appear WITH or WITHOUT explicit comparison words such as 'like', 'as', or 'similar to'.

Text.name: metaphor_step1_decision
Text.value: Mark Yes if an active metaphor is present.

Text.name: metaphor_step1_decision2
Text.value: Mark No otherwise.

Text.name: metaphor_step1_decision3
Text.value: Do not use intermediate scores.

Text.name: metaphor_step2_header
Text.value: 2. CORE METAPHOR TEST (WITH EXAMPLES)

Text.name: metaphor_step2_q
Text.value: Ask: Does the passage DEPEND on a NON-LITERAL conceptual framing that changes how the target concept is understood, explained, or evaluated?

Text.name: metaphor_step2_yes
Text.value: If YES → continue evaluation.

Text.name: metaphor_step2_no
Text.value: If NO → NOT a metaphor (Mark No).

Text.name: metaphor_step2_ex1
Text.value: - 'The theory cannibalizes its own assumptions.' → metaphor

Text.name: metaphor_step2_ex2
Text.value: - 'The theory has internal inconsistencies.' → NOT metaphor

Text.name: metaphor_step3_header
Text.value: 3. NOVELTY & DOMAIN-SHIFT TEST (CRITICAL, WITH EXAMPLES)

Text.name: metaphor_step3_item1
Text.value: Novelty does NOT require original wording.

Text.name: metaphor_step3_item2
Text.value: A metaphor may be ACTIVE if novelty arises from:

Text.name: metaphor_step3_item3
Text.value: - the phrasing itself, OR

Text.name: metaphor_step3_item4
Text.value: - a DOMAIN SHIFT, where a familiar expression is applied to a domain where it is not conventionally used.

Text.name: metaphor_step3_item5
Text.value: HOWEVER: If an expression is idiomatic and used freely across domains, it should be treated as FROZEN and marked No.

Text.name: metaphor_step3_pos_header
Text.value: ✓ Positive examples (Mark Yes):

Text.name: metaphor_step3_pos1
Text.value: - 'She put him in the friend zone so hard that a force field seemed to form around him.' (physics → social interaction)

Text.name: metaphor_step3_neg_header
Text.value: ✗ Negative examples (Mark No):

Text.name: metaphor_step3_neg1
Text.value: - 'That policy change was the final nail in the coffin.' (domain-agnostic idiom)

Text.name: metaphor_step4_header
Text.value: 4. FROZEN / IDIOMATIC METAPHORS (WITH EXAMPLES)

Text.name: metaphor_step4_desc
Text.value: Treat expressions as FROZEN (Mark No) if they are:

Text.name: metaphor_step4_item1
Text.value: - idiomatic and widely recognized

Text.name: metaphor_step4_item2
Text.value: - processed without invoking their source domain

Text.name: metaphor_step4_item3
Text.value: - commonly used across many topics

Text.name: metaphor_step4_ex_header
Text.value: Examples (Mark No):

Text.name: metaphor_step4_ex1
Text.value: - 'tip of the iceberg'

Text.name: metaphor_step4_ex2
Text.value: - 'double-edged sword'

Text.name: metaphor_step4_ex3
Text.value: - 'final nail in the coffin'

Text.name: metaphor_step4_note
Text.value: These do NOT become active merely by appearing in technical, scientific, or abstract contexts.

Text.name: metaphor_step5_header
Text.value: 5. LITERAL FALLBACK TEST (WITH EXAMPLES)

Text.name: metaphor_step5_q
Text.value: Ask: Can the sentence be interpreted fully literally, with no loss of meaning or intent?

Text.name: metaphor_step5_result
Text.value: If YES → NOT a metaphor (Mark No).

Text.name: metaphor_step5_ex1
Text.value: - 'The committee rejected the proposal.' → NOT metaphor

Text.name: metaphor_step5_ex2
Text.value: - 'The proposal was smothered before it could take shape.' → metaphor

Text.name: metaphor_step6_header
Text.value: 6. ABSTRACT METAPHORS (ALLOWED, WITH EXAMPLES)

Text.name: metaphor_step6_item1
Text.value: Metaphors do NOT need to be visual or imagistic.

Text.name: metaphor_step6_item2
Text.value: Abstract metaphors SHOULD be marked Yes if:

Text.name: metaphor_step6_item3
Text.value: - a non-literal source domain is imported

Text.name: metaphor_step6_item4
Text.value: - the framing alters how the concept is understood

Text.name: metaphor_step6_item5
Text.value: - the meaning cannot be preserved under a literal reading

Text.name: metaphor_step6_ex_header
Text.value: Examples (Mark Yes):

Text.name: metaphor_step6_ex1
Text.value: - 'The policy devours the resources it was meant to protect.'

Text.name: metaphor_step6_ex2
Text.value: - 'The algorithm starves certain outcomes of attention.'

Text.name: metaphor_step6_note
Text.value: Abstract, academic, or technical language alone does NOT qualify as metaphor.

Text.name: metaphor_step7_header
Text.value: 7. PERSONIFICATION TEST (WITH EXAMPLES)

Text.name: metaphor_step7_q
Text.value: For personification, ask: Is the attributed action, intention, or behavior clearly impossible or unexpected for the domain?

Text.name: metaphor_step7_yes
Text.value: If YES → metaphor (Mark Yes).

Text.name: metaphor_step7_no
Text.value: If NO → NOT metaphor (Mark No).

Text.name: metaphor_step7_ex1
Text.value: - 'White blood cells ambushing invaders.' → metaphor

Text.name: metaphor_step7_ex2
Text.value: - 'The market responded to new data.' → NOT metaphor

Text.name: metaphor_step8_header
Text.value: 8. METAPHORICAL ANALOGIES (WITH EXAMPLES)

Text.name: metaphor_step8_item1
Text.value: Explicit comparison language ('like', 'similar to', 'think of X as Y', etc.) does NOT exclude a metaphor.

Text.name: metaphor_step8_item2
Text.value: An analogy is ALSO a metaphor if it introduces novel, expressive, or domain-shifting figurative framing, rather than neutral explanation.

Text.name: metaphor_step8_ex1
Text.value: - 'Debugging this problem is like trying to untangle headphones while wearing gloves.' → metaphor

Text.name: metaphor_step8_ex2
Text.value: - 'DNA is like a recipe book.' → NOT metaphor

Text.name: metaphor_step9_header
Text.value: 9. NOT METAPHORS (SUMMARY WITH EXAMPLES)

Text.name: metaphor_step9_desc
Text.value: Always mark No for:

Text.name: metaphor_step9_item1
Text.value: - purely literal descriptions

Text.name: metaphor_step9_item2
Text.value: - standard technical terminology

Text.name: metaphor_step9_item3
Text.value: - metonymy (institutions standing for people)

Text.name: metaphor_step9_item4
Text.value: - shape or visual resemblance only

Text.name: metaphor_step9_item5
Text.value: - routine evaluative or descriptive verbs

Text.name: metaphor_step9_ex_header
Text.value: Examples (Mark No):

Text.name: metaphor_step9_ex1
Text.value: - 'The heart pumps blood.'

Text.name: metaphor_step9_ex2
Text.value: - 'The White House announced new measures.'

Text.name: metaphor_step9_ex3
Text.value: - 'a mushroom-shaped cloud'

Text.name: metaphor_step10_header
Text.value: 10. CONSERVATIVE TIE-BREAKING RULE

Text.name: metaphor_step10_item1
Text.value: When the case is borderline or ambiguous:

Text.name: metaphor_step10_item2
Text.value: - Prefer Mark No over Mark Yes.

Text.name: metaphor_step10_item3
Text.value: - Humans apply a conservative standard; match that standard here.

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_header
Text.value: STEP 1: DEFINITION - What is scaffolding?

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_def
Text.value: Scaffolding means the explanation BUILDS UNDERSTANDING by introducing ideas in order of increasing complexity.

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_q
Text.value: WHAT MAKES AN IDEA 'SIMPLER' vs 'MORE COMPLEX'?

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_cat1
Text.value: 1. STANDALONE vs DEPENDENT:

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_cat1_simple
Text.value: - Simple: 'Atoms are tiny particles' (understood alone)

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_cat1_complex
Text.value: - Complex: 'Electrons orbit the nucleus' (requires knowing what atoms are)

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_cat2
Text.value: 2. FEWER vs MORE PREREQUISITES:

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_cat2_simple
Text.value: - Simple: 'Plants need sunlight' (common knowledge)

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_cat2_complex
Text.value: - Complex: 'Chlorophyll absorbs photons to split water molecules' (requires chemistry background)

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_cat3
Text.value: 3. CONCRETE vs ABSTRACT:

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_cat3_simple
Text.value: - Simple: 'Ice melts when heated' (observable)

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_cat3_complex
Text.value: - Complex: 'Phase transitions occur when thermal energy exceeds intermolecular bonds' (abstract principle)

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_cat4
Text.value: 4. SINGLE vs COMBINED CONCEPTS:

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_cat4_simple
Text.value: - Simple: 'DNA stores genetic information' (one idea)

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_cat4_complex
Text.value: - Complex: 'DNA replication errors during cell division cause mutations that may lead to cancer' (combines 4 concepts)

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_min
Text.value: MINIMUM REQUIREMENT: At least 2 ideas where the second DEPENDS ON or DEEPENS the first.

Text.name: scaffolding_step1_note
Text.value: A SINGLE fact or definition is NOT scaffolding (nothing to build on).

Text.name: scaffolding_step2_header
Text.value: STEP 2: Examples of SCAFFOLDING PRESENT (Mark Yes):

Text.name: scaffolding_step2_short_header
Text.value: SHORT ANSWER examples:

Text.name: scaffolding_step2_short1
Text.value: - 'Cells are the basic building blocks of life. DNA inside cells contains instructions for making proteins.' → First establishes cells, then zooms into DNA - builds from whole to part

Text.name: scaffolding_step2_short2
Text.value: - 'When you heat water, molecules move faster. This is why boiling water evaporates.' → First explains mechanism (molecules), then applies to observable phenomenon

Text.name: scaffolding_step2_short3
Text.value: - 'Gravity pulls things toward Earth. That's why we don't float away.' → First states rule, then connects to everyday experience

Text.name: scaffolding_step2_long_header
Text.value: LONGER ANSWER example:

Text.name: scaffolding_step2_long1
Text.value: - 'Two facts motivate my research—first, diverse systems are healthier... My research asks if it matters that species are being gained and lost... By manipulating plant number and type, I can begin to uncover the mechanisms...' → Starts with motivation → poses question → describes method (clear progression)

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_header
Text.value: STEP 3: Examples of SCAFFOLDING ABSENT (Mark No):

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_single_header
Text.value: SINGLE FACT (nothing to build on):

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_single1
Text.value: - 'Photosynthesis converts sunlight into energy.' → Just one idea, no building possible

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_single2
Text.value: - 'The mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell.' → Single definition, no progression

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_unordered_header
Text.value: UNORDERED LIST of facts:

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_unordered1
Text.value: - 'DNA contains genes. Proteins are made from amino acids. Cells divide through mitosis.' → Multiple facts but no logical order or building between them

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_allatonce_header
Text.value: ALL AT ONCE (no progression):

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_allatonce1
Text.value: - 'Quantum entanglement occurs when particles become correlated such that measuring one instantaneously affects the other regardless of distance due to non-local correlations established at particle creation.' → All concepts crammed together with no build-up

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_complex_header
Text.value: COMPLEX BEFORE SIMPLE:

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_complex1
Text.value: - 'The non-local correlations from entanglement happen because... basically, particles can be connected.' → Starts with the hard part, then gives the simple explanation

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_flow_header
Text.value: LOGICAL FLOW WITHOUT BUILDING (NOT scaffolding):

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_flow1
Text.value: - 'Scientists collected samples. They analyzed the samples. They published their findings.' → Ideas flow logically but stay at same complexity level - no building

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_flow2
Text.value: - 'The experiment tested temperature. Results showed higher temps increased reaction speed. This confirmed the hypothesis.' → Coherent narrative, but each sentence is equally complex - no scaffolding

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_flow3
Text.value: - 'Photosynthesis happens in leaves. It uses sunlight. Plants need it to survive.' → Related facts that flow, but none requires understanding the previous one

Text.name: scaffolding_step3_key
Text.value: KEY DISTINCTION: Scaffolding requires INCREASING DEPTH, not just logical coherence.

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_header
Text.value: STEP 4: Common edge cases:

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_short_header
Text.value: SHORT ≠ NO SCAFFOLDING:

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_short1
Text.value: - A 2-sentence answer CAN have scaffolding if idea #1 prepares for idea #2

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_short2
Text.value: - Length doesn't matter; logical ordering does

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_trans_header
Text.value: TRANSITION WORDS DON'T GUARANTEE SCAFFOLDING:

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_trans1
Text.value: - 'because', 'therefore', 'this means' can indicate building, but not always

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_with_yes_header
Text.value: WITH transitions, IS scaffolding:

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_with_yes1
Text.value: - 'Gravity pulls objects toward Earth. Because of this, dropped objects fall.' → Simple rule first, then applies it (builds)

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_with_no_header
Text.value: WITH transitions, NOT scaffolding:

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_with_no1
Text.value: - 'Entropy increases because systems tend toward disorder because energy spreads out.' → 'because' used twice but all concepts at same complexity level (no building)

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_with_no2
Text.value: - 'Quantum tunneling occurs because wavefunctions extend beyond barriers.' → Single complex statement, transition word doesn't help

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_without_yes_header
Text.value: WITHOUT transitions, IS scaffolding:

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_without_yes1
Text.value: - 'Atoms have electrons. Electrons carry charge. Charge creates electricity.' → Clear simple→complex progression despite no explicit connectors

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_chrono_header
Text.value: CHRONOLOGICAL ORDER ≠ SCAFFOLDING:

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_chrono1
Text.value: - 'First I added water, then I heated it, then it boiled' is just a sequence

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_chrono2
Text.value: - Scaffolding requires conceptual building, not just time order

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_logical_header
Text.value: LOGICAL FLOW ≠ SCAFFOLDING:

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_logical1
Text.value: - A well-organized answer can flow smoothly without scaffolding

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_logical2
Text.value: - Scaffolding requires each idea to be MORE COMPLEX than the previous

Text.name: scaffolding_step4_logical3
Text.value: - If all ideas are at the same complexity level, it's NOT scaffolding (even if coherent)
